passages.title: The Lost Kite
passages.text:
On the morning of Makar Sankranti, the sky above Pune was full of kites. Meera's kite was red with a long yellow tail. It soared above the rooftops, higher than any other kite on the street. Then a strong gust of wind tugged at the string. Snap! The kite drifted away over the trees.

Meera was crestfallen. Her shoulders dropped and she stared at the empty sky without a word. Her brother Rohan tried to console her. He put an arm around her and promised to help her make a new kite. That afternoon they collected paper, thin sticks and glue. By evening the new kite was ready, and Meera's smile came back.

passages.title: Frogs of the Western Ghats
passages.text:
The Western Ghats are a long chain of hills near Pune. In the monsoon, the forests here become a home for many kinds of frogs. Some of these frogs are so minute that one could sit on your fingernail. Others are as long as your hand.

Many of these frogs are nocturnal. They sleep under wet leaves all day and come out to hunt insects after dark. A few kinds are very rare. Scientists have found them in only one valley and nowhere else in the world.

When the rains end, the forest becomes parched. The streams dry up and the soil cracks in the heat. The frogs dig deep into the earth and stay there, still and quiet, until the next monsoon arrives.

passages.title: Diwali at Nani's House
passages.text:
Every year we travel to Nani's house in Nashik for Diwali. This year the journey felt endless, but at last the auto-rickshaw stopped at her gate. Nani was delighted to see us and hugged us tightly. Her house is enormous, with a wide courtyard and a tall mango tree.

That evening my cousin Tara and I made a rangoli by the door. We used bright pink, glowing orange and deep blue powder. When we lit the diyas, the whole courtyard sparkled. I felt so cheerful that I could not stop smiling. Later, Nani served us warm, delicious laddoos.

passages.title: A Busy Saturday
passages.text:
On Saturday, Grandpa woke me early. 'Be good while we are at the market,' he told my younger brother Dev. Dev nodded and sat quietly with his crayons.

At the market Grandpa bought fresh spinach, ripe bananas and a bag of rice. The bag was heavy, so I helped him carry it to the auto-rickshaw. On the way home the sky turned dark and the wind began to howl. We were terrified that the storm would catch us, but we reached home just in time. Dev was scared too. He had hidden under the table with his crayons.

That night I had a fever. Grandpa gave me some good medicine and a warm glass of haldi milk. By morning I felt well again, and I was thankful for such a caring grandfather.

passages.title: Our Trip to the Hills
passages.text:
Last May our class went on a school trip to Mahabaleshwar. The winding road climbed through thick green forest. Tall, silent trees leaned over the bus like curious giants. Grey monkeys chattered in the branches as we drove past.

At the top, a cool, misty breeze touched our faces. We walked to a rocky viewpoint above a deep valley. Far below, a silver stream twisted between the hills, and tiny houses with red roofs dotted the fields.

For lunch we sat on a soft, grassy slope and opened our tiffins. The air smelt of wet earth and ripe strawberries. Before we left, our educator bought each of us a cup of fresh strawberry cream. It was cold, sweet and smooth, the perfect end to a happy day. All the way down the hill, we sang songs on the bus.

passages.title: The Monsoon Night
passages.text:
It was the first night of the monsoon. Kavya lay in bed and listened. Drip, drip, drip went the water from the leaking gutter. Outside, the wind howled around the building and the window rattled in its frame. Somewhere down the lane, a dog barked twice.

Suddenly there was a flash of light. Crash! Thunder shook the whole house. Kavya pulled her blanket over her head. Then she heard a soft creak as the door opened. It was Papa with a torch.

'The power has gone,' he whispered. Together they lit a candle. Its flame hissed for a moment and then glowed steadily. Kavya listened to the rain drumming on the roof. Tick-tock went the old clock on the wall. Soon her eyes closed, and she fell fast asleep.

passages.title: Diwali Morning
passages.text: On Diwali morning, Tara leapt out of bed before the sun was up. The whole house smelt of sweet ladoos and fresh marigolds. Her grandmother was humming softly as she drew a dazzling rangoli by the front door. Tara knelt beside her and sprinkled bright pink powder into the petals. "It looks magnificent," whispered her little brother, his eyes wide. Then the whole family sat down together to a breakfast of crispy puris and spicy potatoes.

passages.title: Our Trip to Sinhagad
passages.text: Last week our class visited Sinhagad Fort near Pune. Our bus wound its way up the steep hill, and we gasped at the misty valley far below. At the top, the wind howled around the ancient stone walls. Our guide, Mr Pawar, told us thrilling stories about brave soldiers who climbed the cliffs in the dark. After that we sat on the grass and gobbled our tiffin. Ananya had a lot of grapes, so she shared them with everyone. It was a nice day, and on the way down we were all exhausted but happy.

passages.title: The Rain Comes to Pune
passages.text: For weeks the city had baked under a fierce sun. The ground cracked, the leaves drooped, and even the stray dogs lay panting in the shade. Then one afternoon the sky turned the colour of ink. Thunder rumbled over the hills, and a cool wind swept through the lanes. Zoya got her umbrella and ran outside. Fat raindrops splattered on the roof, and soon the rain was pounding the streets. Children splashed through puddles, shrieking with joy. Their neighbour, Mrs D'Souza, threw open her window and laughed. The air smelt of wet earth and new leaves, and even the old banyan tree seemed to dance. Zoya's mother fried a lot of crispy pakoras, and the whole family sat together by the window to watch the storm. It was a nice evening, and nobody wanted the rain to stop.

passages.title: A Letter About Holi
passages.text:
Dear Kabir,

I hope you are well in Nagpur. I wanted to tell you all about Holi at our building in Pune this year. It was really nice. The drums boomed all morning, and everyone came down to the garden with buckets of coloured water. My friend Sana got a water pistol and chased me round the swings until I was purple from head to toe. "Got you!" she shrieked, and we both fell over laughing. Grandpa sat on a bench in the shade and chuckled at us. When Aunty Farah splashed him with green, he only muttered, "Not again," and wiped his glasses. We had a really nice time and got a lot of colour on our clothes. Later we ate gujiya and drank cool thandai under the mango tree. The food was nice. By the evening my hands were still pink and my hair was blue. Mum says it will wash out in a week. I wish you could come next year, because it would be so much fun with you here.

Love from,
Diya

passages.title: The Night Market
passages.text: Every Friday, the night market on Laxmi Road wakes up as the sun goes down. Stalls glow like a string of fireflies along the street. Sizzling samosas spit and crackle in huge pans, and the smell drifts through the crowd. Near the corner, a man sells roasted corn to a long queue of children. Aman likes the bangle stall best. The bangles clink and jingle as the seller stacks them, and they shine as bright as rainbows under the lamps. Grandpa holds Aman's hand tightly, his fingers as rough as tree bark. A tired dog dozes under a cart, curled up like a cushion. "Stay close," says Grandpa, as the crowd pushes and swirls like a river around them. By ten o'clock, Aman's bag is full of bangles and his feet are sore, but his heart is light.

passages.title: Monsoon on the Ghats
passages.text:
The dark clouds came marching over the hills,
grey and heavy, a herd of elephants,
trunk to tail and trunk to tail,
till the whole wide sky sagged low with rain.

Then the drops began to drum,
drip, drip, drumming on the dusty road,
pattering on the peepal leaves,
plopping into puddles in the lane.

The river woke and rushed and roared,
racing like a runaway train,
carrying sticks and leaves and stones
down, down to the valley floor.

My grandmother likes to sit and watch,
her shawl wrapped round her shoulders tight.
"The earth is drinking," she says to me,
"as thirsty as a traveller after a long walk."

The frogs began their croaking choir,
as loud as a band at a wedding feast,
and the peacock spread his shimmering tail
like a fan of green and gold.

By night the world was washed and new,
the air as fresh as a mint leaf,
and I fell asleep to the soft, slow song
of rain still singing on the roof.

passages.title: Motu Escapes
passages.text: Motu the goat lived behind Mrs Joshi's house in a small pen made of old wooden planks. Every morning he chewed his breakfast of leaves and stared at the busy lane beyond the gate. One Tuesday, the milkman forgot to close the latch. Motu got out of the pen and into the lane. He trotted past the tea stall, sniffed at a basket of guavas, and then, with a happy bleat, he charged straight into the vegetable market. Tomatoes tumbled from the carts. A shopkeeper yelled and flapped his arms. Children shrieked with laughter as Motu bounded from stall to stall, his bell jangling. Mrs Joshi heard the noise and hurried down the lane, her slippers slapping on the road. She found Motu munching a cabbage as if nothing had happened. "You naughty goat!" she scolded, but she was smiling. She took his rope and led him home, while the whole market clapped and cheered. That evening, Mrs Joshi fixed a new lock on the gate, and Motu sulked in his pen all night.

passages.title: Kites on the Roof
passages.text:
It was Makar Sankranti, and the sky over Pune was full of kites. Arjun climbed up to the roof with his sister Kavya. Their kite was green with a long yellow tail.
"Is the wind strong enough?" asked Kavya.
"Yes, it is," said Arjun. "Hold the string tightly!"
Kavya let go of the kite and it rose above the water tanks. "How high our kite is flying!" she laughed.
Then a red kite swooped close. "Watch out for that red one," said Arjun. "Pull the string to the left."
"Will our kite be cut?" asked Kavya.
The green kite danced away just in time. Below them, Aai called up the stairs. "Come down for til laddoos when you are hungry."
"What a wonderful day this is!" said Arjun.

passages.title: The Lost Tiffin
passages.text:
Meher opened her school bag and looked inside. "My tiffin box has gone!" she cried.
Her friend Zoya put down her pencil. "Did you leave it on the bus?" she asked.
"No, I had it in assembly," said Meher.
The two girls searched under the desks and behind the cupboard. They even looked in the reading corner. Just then, Joshi Sir walked in with a blue box in his hand.
"Is this yours, Meher?" he asked with a smile. "I found it next to the water cooler."
Meher clapped her hands. "Thank you so much!" she said.
At lunch, she shared her poha with Zoya, and they laughed about the tiffin box that went for a walk.

passages.title: Waiting for the Bus
passages.text:
On the morning of the school trip to the science park, the whole class waited at the gate. Tanvi kept looking at the clock above the office door. "If the bus comes soon," she said, "we will be the first class there."
Kunal told her that the bus was stuck in traffic near the station. Tanvi sighed and sat down on her bag.
"Never mind," said Varun, "we can play a word game while we wait."
They played until a horn sounded at the end of the road. "Here it comes!" shouted Kunal.
On the bus, Ms Pillai counted the children twice. She said that nobody should stand while the bus was moving. "Is everyone sitting down?" she asked.
"Yes, Ms Pillai!" they all called back.
At the science park, Varun ran straight to the giant magnet. "This is the best trip ever," he said, and nobody disagreed.

passages.title: Our Trip to the Science Centre
passages.text:
On Tuesday, Class 4B went on a trip to the science centre in Pimpri. We left school at eight o'clock, and everyone sang songs on the bus while Mrs Kulkarni checked her list. Since it was the first trip of the year, we were all very excited.

However, the trip did not begin well. A big tree had fallen across the road after the night's storm, so the bus had to turn back and find another way. We waited for almost an hour before we reached the gate.

Meanwhile, the guide at the centre had kept the planet show ready for us. She said we could still watch it so that we did not miss the best part. Inside the dark dome, the stars moved slowly over our heads.

As a result of the delay, we ate our tiffin on the lawn instead of in the hall. Nobody minded, because the sun was shining and a cool wind was blowing from the hills.

Later that afternoon, we tried the hands-on rooms. The giant bubble would not rise unless you pressed the red button, and Farhan pressed it so many times that even the guide laughed.

passages.title: How to Make a Paper Lantern for Diwali
passages.text:
You will need: a sheet of coloured card, a ruler, a pencil, a pair of scissors, glue and a thin strip of paper for the handle.

1. First, fold the card neatly in half along its long side.
2. With the ruler and pencil, draw straight lines across the fold, about two centimetres apart.
3. Carefully cut along each line from the folded edge. Stop a little way before the open edge, or the lantern will fall apart.
4. Gently open the card and roll it into a tube. Glue the two short edges together firmly. After ten minutes, check that the join is strong.
5. Hang the lantern.
6. Leave the glue to dry overnight before you put anything inside the lantern.

Tip: Work slowly at the table, not on the floor, so that the scissors stay safe. Always ask an adult for help when you use sharp tools. Paper lanterns look best when you hang several of them in a row across the doorway, where everyone who visits can see them.

passages.title: Riya's Kite
passages.text: On Sunday morning, Riya took her red kite to the terrace. Her grandfather tied a long string to it. The wind was strong, and the kite flew higher than the water tank. A green parrot sat on the wall and watched. At noon, Riya's mother called them down for hot poha and sweet lassi.

passages.title: The Class 3 Garden
passages.text: Class 3 at Sunrise School in Pune has a small garden behind the library. The children planted tomatoes, chillies and marigolds in June, just before the monsoon. Every morning, two children water the plants with a green watering can. Mr Deshpande, the gardener, shows them how to pull out weeds. In October, the class picked forty tomatoes. They gave half of them to the school kitchen for the lunch dal.

passages.title: Sports Day
passages.text: Sports Day at Green Valley School was held on a cool Saturday in December. The events began at eight o'clock with the flag march. Class 3 ran the sack race first, and Aarav from 3B won it. Next came the lemon-and-spoon race. Zoya dropped her lemon twice but still finished third. After a short break for bananas and water, the older children played kabaddi on the big ground. The Red House beat the Blue House by six points. At the end, the principal gave out the prizes. Every child who took part got a small badge shaped like a star. The Yellow House won the shield because it had the most points from all the races.

passages.title: Welcome to Tulsi Butterfly Park
passages.text: Welcome to Tulsi Butterfly Park, on the edge of Pune. The park is open from Tuesday to Sunday, from nine in the morning until five in the evening. It is closed on Mondays so that the gardeners can trim the plants. More than sixty kinds of butterflies visit the park. The best time to see them is between ten and twelve, when the sun has warmed their wings. Butterflies cannot fly well when they are cold. Please walk slowly on the paths and do not touch the wings, because the tiny scales come off easily. Tickets cost twenty rupees for children and forty rupees for adults. School groups of more than twenty children get in free if they book a week before. Water bottles are allowed, but please take your plastic wrappers home with you.

passages.title: Kabir Helps
passages.text: Kabir was the smallest boy in Class 3, but he was always the first to help. When Meera dropped her crayons, he picked them up. When the new girl sat alone at lunch, he shared his tiffin of aloo paratha with her. He grinned and said, "There is always enough for one more."

passages.title: The Thursday Market
passages.text: Every Thursday, the market near Amma's house filled up with stalls. Under blue plastic sheets, the sellers piled up shiny green chillies, heaps of purple brinjals and baskets of wet, dark jamuns. The ground was muddy from the rain, and the air smelled of roasting corn. A radio crackled somewhere, playing old film songs. Children splashed through the puddles while their mothers bargained loudly. Nisha held Amma's hand tightly. She had never seen so many people in one place, and she did not let go once.

passages.title: Mr Joshi's Bookshop
passages.text: Mr Joshi's bookshop was squeezed between a sweet shop and a tailor on a narrow lane in old Pune. Inside, it was dim and cool. Books were stacked from the floor to the ceiling, and some piles leaned like tired trees. A fan creaked slowly above the counter. Mr Joshi himself was tiny, with round glasses and a grey moustache that twitched when he laughed. He knew where every book was, even in the tallest piles. When Arjun asked for a book about snakes, Mr Joshi closed his eyes, tapped his chin twice and walked straight to a shelf near the back. "Third pile, fifth book," he said proudly, and pulled it out without dropping a single one.

passages.title: The Storm at Harnai
passages.text:
At dawn, the beach at Harnai was calm and silver. Small waves whispered against the fishing boats, and gulls drifted lazily over the water. Salim's grandfather mended his net, humming softly. Salim was bored. "Nothing ever happens here," he grumbled, kicking at the sand.

By noon, the sky had turned the colour of a bruise. The wind howled and threw sand into their eyes. The waves grew tall and angry, crashing over the rocks. Grandfather stopped humming. He shouted to the other fishermen, and together they dragged the boats up the beach, away from the water.

Salim did not grumble now. He pulled at the ropes until his hands stung. When the last boat was safe, Grandfather put an arm round him. "Today you worked like a real fisherman," he said. Salim grinned, even though he was soaked to the skin.

passages.title: Holi Morning
passages.text: On Holi morning, Tara filled her water balloons. Then she ran outside and threw pink powder at her brother. He chased her round the garden with a water gun. Soon they were both wet and pink. At lunchtime, Mum gave them hot puran poli, and they ate it on the steps.

passages.title: Our Trip to the Planetarium
passages.text: Last Friday, Class 3 went on a school trip to the planetarium. First, we climbed into a big yellow bus outside the school gate. The ride took an hour because of the traffic. When we arrived, a guide called Mrs Rao led us into a round, dark room. We lay back in our seats and looked up at the dome. Suddenly, thousands of stars appeared above us! After the show, we ate our tiffin on the lawn. Then we sang songs all the way back to school.

passages.title: The Lost Cricket Ball
passages.text: Dev hit the ball so hard that it flew over the wall and landed in Mrs Kulkarni's garden. The boys groaned. Mrs Kulkarni was known for her temper and her prize roses. Nobody wanted to knock on her door, so Dev went alone. His knees shook as he rang the bell. To his surprise, Mrs Kulkarni smiled. "I used to play cricket when I was a girl," she said. She handed back the ball and gave him four ladoos for his team. The next Sunday, the boys invited her to umpire their match. She wore a big straw hat and shouted "Out!" louder than anyone.

passages.title: The Rangoli Competition
passages.text: The night before Diwali, our housing society held a rangoli competition. Ishita and her little brother Om chose a peacock design. Ishita drew the outline with white chalk while Om sorted the colours into small bowls. They had almost finished the tail when a sudden gust of wind blew across the courtyard. Half of the blue powder scattered over the tiles. Om began to cry. Ishita wanted to cry too, but she looked at the mess and had an idea. She swept the scattered blue into the shape of a river flowing past the peacock's feet. Then she added tiny yellow diyas along its banks. When the judges came round, they stopped at the peacock for a long time. "A peacock beside a river of light," said one. "Nobody else thought of that." Ishita and Om won second prize, and Om stopped crying at once.

passages.title: Bablu the Brave Bus
passages.text: Bablu is the oldest bus in Pune. His paint is peeling and his horn goes PAARP! The other buses laugh at him. But one rainy night, when the roads flood, only Bablu is brave enough to carry the children home. A funny, warm story for young readers who love vehicles and heroes.

passages.title: Two Books on the Library Shelf
passages.text:
Book A: The Secret of the Fort
Meher and her cousin find an old map in their grandmother's trunk. It leads them to a hidden room inside an old hill fort. Who left the map there, and why? A mystery full of clues and surprises.

Book B: Wonderful Elephants
How much does an elephant eat in a day? Why do elephants flap their ears? This book is packed with photographs and facts about elephants in India's forests.

passages.title: The Girl Who Talked to Clouds
passages.text:
Blurb: Every afternoon, Asha climbs to her rooftop in Nashik and talks to the clouds. Nobody believes her when she says the clouds talk back. Then, one dry summer, the rain does not come, and the whole town is worried. Can Asha persuade the clouds to help? A magical story about friendship, patience and the monsoon.

Review by Kiran, aged 9: I read this book in two days because I could not stop! My favourite part is when Asha has a picnic on the roof with a tiny grey cloud. The middle was a little slow, but the ending made me smile. I would give it four stars.

passages.title: Book Corner
passages.text:
Book 1: Rhymes from the Railway
Twenty short, funny poems about life on Indian trains: the tea seller's song, the sleepy uncle on the top berth and the goat that bought a ticket. Each poem has a bright picture beside it. Perfect for reading aloud with a friend, one short poem at a time.

Book 2: Captain Kesar and the Space Mango
When a giant mango lands on Kesar's farm, she finds it is really a spaceship! A fast, exciting adventure across the stars, with a chapter that ends on a cliffhanger every time.

Review of Book 2 by Mrs Pillai, school librarian: Children who enjoy action will race through this book. However, the chapters are long, so it suits confident readers more than those just starting chapter books.

passages.title: Tiffin Time
passages.text: Lunch boxes in Class 3 are full of different foods. Simran brings rice and rajma. Joseph brings idli with coconut chutney. Farah often has a cheese sandwich, and Mohit loves his mother's methi paratha. At lunch, the children like to swap a little of their food, so everyone tastes something new.

passages.title: Auto-rickshaws
passages.text: Auto-rickshaws are one of the most common ways to travel in Indian towns. They have three wheels and a small roof, and many are painted yellow and black or green and yellow. An auto-rickshaw can carry about three passengers, though families sometimes squeeze in more. Because they are small, autos can weave through busy streets where buses cannot go. Many people take an auto to the station, to the market or to school. In Pune, you can hear their engines buzzing on almost every road.

passages.title: Clean-Up Day
passages.text: On Saturday morning, the air on Vetal Hill smelled of wet earth after the night's rain. Thirty children from our school climbed the path with sacks and gloves. We were there for one reason: to clean up the hill. Visitors had left plastic bottles, crisp packets and even an old shoe among the bushes. We worked in pairs, and every pair filled at least two sacks. A forest guard showed us how to sort the rubbish, so that the bottles could be recycled. By lunchtime, the paths looked fresh and green again. We were tired and muddy, but we felt proud that the hill was clean.

passages.title: Bridges That Grow
passages.text:
In the hills of Meghalaya, in north-east India, some bridges are not built from wood or stone. They are grown from living trees. Villagers guide the roots of rubber fig trees across a stream, tying them to bamboo poles or old tree trunks. Slowly, over many years, the roots grow thick and strong and reach the other side. Then the villagers press stones into the gaps to make a path.

A bridge of wood can rot and a bridge of steel can rust in the heavy rain, but a root bridge does the opposite. Because the tree is still alive, its roots keep growing, so the bridge gets stronger as it gets older. Some root bridges are so old that nobody remembers who first started them. Today, visitors walk across them, and the village children learn how to care for them, so that the bridges will last for many more years.

passages.title: The Red Kite
passages.text:
Riya had made the red kite with her nani. On Sunday she flew it high above the roof. Then the string snapped.
The kite floated away over the mango trees. Riya stood very still. Her lip shook. She did not say a word on the
way home, and at dinner she only pushed her poha around her plate.

passages.title: Picked Last
passages.text:
At break, the boys chose teams for cricket. Sahil was picked first, then Dev, then Imran. Arjun was picked last
of all. His face went hot. He kicked a stone and looked down at his shoes. In the last over, the ball flew high
towards him. Arjun ran, stretched out both hands and held on. His team cheered and lifted him up. Arjun grinned
all the way back to class, and he kept the ball on his desk until the bell rang.

passages.title: The Big Diya
passages.text:
Two days before Diwali, Kabir was helping Aai set out the clay diyas on the balcony. When she went inside to
fetch the oil, his elbow knocked the biggest diya off the ledge. It cracked into three pieces. Kabir looked at the
door. Quickly, he pushed the pieces behind the flower pots and began to whistle.
"Where is the big diya, the one Ajoba painted?" asked Aai when she came back.
"I don't know," said Kabir, without looking up. His ears turned pink.
That night Kabir could not sleep. He turned one way, then the other. At last he crept into the kitchen, where Aai
was making chaklis, and held out his hand. The three pieces lay on his palm.

passages.title: Not Yet
passages.text:
Meera's family moved from Pune to Kolkata in the middle of the monsoon. On her first morning at the new school,
Meera wore her neatest uniform. "I'm not nervous at all," she told Baba at the gate, but she held his hand so
tightly that his fingers went white.
In class, the children spoke Bengali to each other and laughed at jokes she did not understand. Meera opened her
tiffin and closed it again without eating. At lunch, a girl with two long plaits sat down beside her. "I'm
Tanushree," she said. "Do you play carrom?" Meera nodded.
That evening Baba asked, "Well? Shall we go back to Pune?" Meera was already setting up the carrom board on the
floor. "Not yet," she said. "Tanushree is coming on Saturday."

passages.title: One Umbrella
passages.text:
It was the first day of the monsoon. Anu had a big blue umbrella, but her friend Zoya had none. "Come under
mine," said Anu, and they walked to school together, laughing. The next morning Anu forgot her umbrella at home.
Zoya ran up with a new yellow one. "Come under mine," she said.

passages.title: Ten Rupees Too Many
passages.text:
Tara went to Mr Pawar's shop to buy milk. She paid with a fifty-rupee note. Mr Pawar was busy and gave her
thirty-four rupees back. Outside, Tara counted the coins. The milk cost twenty-six rupees, so he had given her
ten rupees too many. Nobody had seen. She could buy a guava with it. Tara turned round, walked back into the shop
and put the ten rupees on the counter. "You gave me too much," she said. Mr Pawar smiled. "Thank you, Tara. Not
many people would do that."

passages.title: The Mango at the Top
passages.text:
High on the old tree hung the last mango of summer. Monkey climbed up, but the branch was too thin and he slid
back down. Parrot flew up and pecked at the stalk, but the mango was too heavy to carry. Tortoise sat at the
bottom and said nothing for a long time.
At last he spoke. "Monkey, climb as far as you safely can and shake the branch. Parrot, peck the stalk while it
shakes. I will wait below on this soft grass."
The branch shook, the stalk broke, and the mango dropped onto the grass beside Tortoise without a bruise. The
three friends cut it into three pieces and ate it in the shade.

passages.title: Ajoba's Old Bat
passages.text:
For his birthday, Dhruv hoped for a shiny new cricket bat like the one in the sports shop window. Instead, Ajoba
gave him his own old bat. The handle was wrapped in faded green tape, and the wood was dark and covered in little
dents.
"Thank you," said Dhruv quietly, and he hid the bat under his bed.
On Saturday, Dhruv's team was short of a bat. He had no choice. He walked onto the ground with the old one, and
some of the boys giggled. Then the first ball came. Crack! It flew over the wall. The old wood was heavy and
strong, and Dhruv hit four more boundaries that morning.
When he got home, he sat beside Ajoba. "Tell me about every dent," he said. Ajoba laughed and began with the very
first one.

passages.title: Two Thirsty Birds
passages.text:
Telling 1: A thirsty crow found a pot with a little water at the bottom. He dropped stones in, one by one, until
the water rose. Then he drank.
Telling 2: A thirsty sparrow found a pot in a garden. She dropped stones in, one by one, until the water rose.
Then she drank.

passages.title: The Monkey and the Crocodile, Twice
passages.text:
Telling 1: A crocodile carried his friend the monkey across the river on his back. Halfway, he said, "My wife
wants to eat your heart." The monkey said, "I left my heart in the jamun tree. Take me back!" On the bank, the
monkey leapt into the tree and never rode on the crocodile again.
Telling 2: A crocodile carried his friend the monkey across the river. Halfway, he said, "I am taking you to my
wife for dinner." The monkey said, "I left my heart in the jamun tree." Back on the bank, the crocodile felt
ashamed and said sorry, and the two friends shared jamuns every evening.

passages.title: The Hare and the Lion: Two Tellings
passages.text:
Telling 1, from a village: A lion ate one animal every day. One morning it was the hare's turn. The hare walked
slowly and arrived late. "Another lion stopped me," he said. "He says this forest is his." The lion roared, "Show
me!" The hare led him to a deep well. The lion looked in, saw his own face, and jumped in to fight it. The animals
were safe.
Telling 2, from a city book: A tiger ordered the animals to bring him food every day. A small hare was sent with a
basket of fruit. "A bigger tiger took the rest," she said, and she led him to a still pond. The tiger saw himself,
growled, and dived in. He climbed out wet and embarrassed, and he never bullied anyone again.

passages.title: The Greedy Dog, Then and Now
passages.text:
Telling 1, told long ago in a village: A dog stole a bone from the butcher and ran off with it. To get home he
had to cross a narrow wooden bridge over a stream. Halfway across, he looked down and saw another dog in the water
with a bigger bone. "I want that one too," he thought, and he barked at it. His own bone fell into the stream and
floated away.
Telling 2, written this year in Pune: A street dog grabbed a vada pav from a stall on Laxmi Road and raced off.
After the monsoon rain, the footpath was full of puddles. In one shiny puddle he saw a dog holding a bigger vada
pav. He barked to scare it. Splash! His vada pav fell in the puddle and turned to mush. He walked home hungry.

passages.title: Priya's Seed
passages.text:
Priya found a tamarind seed in her tiffin box. She pressed it into a pot of soil on her window. Every morning
before school, she gave it a cup of water. Then the monsoon came, and rain fell on the pot every day. One morning
Priya saw something tiny and green in the soil.

passages.title: Om and the Squirrel
passages.text:
On Sankranti, Om was flying kites on the terrace when he saw a squirrel caught in some old kite string. It was
wriggling and squeaking. Om knelt down and gently cut the string with his mother's small scissors. The squirrel
ran up the neem tree and looked back at him.
A week later, Om's best kite got stuck high in the same neem tree. Its string was wound round a thin branch that
no one could reach. Om sat on the step and sighed. Then he heard a scratching sound in the leaves above him.

passages.title: The Race to the Banyan Tree
passages.text:
Every year the children of Wadi village raced from the school gate to the old banyan tree. Neel was the fastest
runner in the village, and he knew it. "I could win this race with my eyes shut," he told everyone.
Farah was small and slow, but she practised every evening, running a little further each time.
On race day, Neel shot ahead. By the halfway point, Farah was far behind. Neel looked back and laughed. He stopped
at a cart to buy a cold lassi and sat in the shade to drink it. "Plenty of time," he said, and closed his eyes.
Farah kept running, step after step, without stopping once. Soon she could see the banyan tree.

passages.title: The Missing Ladoos
passages.text:
On the morning of Ganesh Chaturthi, Aaji made twelve besan ladoos and left them on a plate by the kitchen window
to cool. Then she went to the temple with Ajoba. They were away all morning.
At lunchtime, Sunil ran into the kitchen. The plate had only four ladoos left. There were yellow crumbs along the
window sill, and the window was wide open. On the mango tree outside, the leaves were shaking, though there was no
wind.
"Was it you, Sunil?" asked his sister Gauri. Sunil showed his hands. They were clean, and he had been at cricket
practice since breakfast.
Just then, they heard a happy chattering sound from the tree. A small brown face peeped out between the leaves,
with yellow crumbs on its whiskers.

passages.title: Mango Lassi for Two
passages.text:
You need: one ripe mango, two cups of curd, two spoons of sugar, some ice.
1. Peel the mango and cut it into pieces.
2. Put the mango pieces in a jug.
3. Add the curd and the sugar.
4. Blend until smooth.
5. Pour into two glasses and add the ice.

passages.title: The Classroom Treasure Hunt
passages.text:
Our class has hidden a box of rangoli colours. Follow these steps to find it.
1. Start at the school gate.
2. Walk straight past the banyan tree.
3. Turn left at the water tap.
4. Go up the steps to the library.
5. Look under the second bench on your right.
6. Bring the box back to your educator.

passages.title: Bhel Puri for Four
passages.text:
You need: four cups of puffed rice, one onion, one tomato, green chutney, sweet tamarind chutney, half a lemon and
a cup of sev.
First, ask an adult to chop the onion and the tomato into small pieces.
Before you add any chutney, mix the puffed rice with the onion and tomato in a big bowl.
Next, add two spoons of each chutney and stir well.
Squeeze the lemon over the top after the chutney.
Do not add the sev until just before you eat, or it will go soft. Scatter it on top and serve straight away.

passages.title: Word Magic
passages.text:
Word Magic is a puzzle that turns one word into another. Read every step before you start, and write each new word
on a new line so that you can check your work afterwards.
1. Write the word PAN.
2. Write the same letters backwards.
3. Put the letter S at the front of your word.
4. Change the A to an I.
5. Read your new word aloud.
If your word is not a real word, go back to the first step and try again, one step at a time. A real word means
you have followed every step. Then make up your own Word Magic puzzle and give it to a friend to try. Ask a
grown-up or a friend to check your words.

passages.title: Come to the Mango Fair!
passages.text:
Come to the Mango Fair! It is at the town hall on Saturday 12 May. Tickets cost twenty rupees. There are ten kinds
of mango to taste. Our mangoes are the sweetest in the world! Every child gets one free mango. It will be the best
day of your summer.

passages.title: Our Trip to Sinhagad Fort
passages.text:
On Friday, Class 3 went on a trip to Sinhagad Fort, near Pune. We left school at seven o'clock in two buses. The
climb to the top took us two hours. Mrs Kulkarni carried a first-aid box and a big bag of bananas. At the top we
ate kanda bhaji and drank cold buttermilk. I think the bhaji there is the tastiest food in the world. The view
from the top was amazing. We were back at school by four o'clock. It was the best trip we have ever had.

passages.title: All About Kabaddi
passages.text:
Kabaddi is a team game that is played all over India. Each team has seven players on the court. One player, the
raider, runs into the other team's half and tries to tag as many players as possible. While raiding, the raider
must keep saying "kabaddi, kabaddi" without stopping for breath. If the raider is caught, the other team wins a
point. Kabaddi is far more exciting than any other sport. You do not need a bat or a ball, only a flat piece of
ground. Every school should have a kabaddi team. Children who play kabaddi are the bravest children of all.

passages.title: A Letter to the Town Newsletter
passages.text:
Dear Editor,
I am writing about the new bus that now runs from our village to the town school. The bus leaves the village at
half past seven every morning and stops at five places on the way. It has thirty seats and a ramp for wheelchairs.
Before the bus came, many children walked for over an hour to reach school.
In my view, this bus is the most important thing to happen to our village in years. The drivers are the
friendliest people in the whole district. The bus costs ten rupees a day for each child. Some parents say that is
too much, but I believe it is worth every paisa. Everyone in the village should thank the council.
Yours faithfully,
Mrs S. Deshmukh

passages.title: Kavya's tiffin
passages.text: Every morning, Kavya's grandmother packs her tiffin before the school bus comes at half past seven. On Monday she packed poha with peanuts and a small banana. On Tuesday there were two parathas and a spoonful of mango pickle. Kavya likes Wednesday best, because that is the day of idli and coconut chutney. She always saves one idli for her friend Ritu, who sits next to her in class and never has time for breakfast at home.
