passages.title: The terrace garden at Sunrise School
passages.text: Three years ago, the flat roof of Sunrise School in Pune was empty and hot. Today it is covered with pots and long wooden boxes full of soil. The Grade 4 children look after the garden. Each class has its own box, and every Friday two children from each class water the plants and pull out the weeds. They grow tomatoes, spinach, chillies and mint. In June, before the monsoon starts, the children cover the boxes with old cotton sheets so that the heavy rain does not wash the soil away. Last year the garden gave so many tomatoes that the school cook made tomato soup for everyone in the school on Children's Day.

passages.title: The lost kite
passages.text:
On the morning of Makar Sankranti, Arjun climbed to the roof of his building in Kothrud with his cousin Neha. Arjun carried a green kite with a long yellow tail, which his father had bought from the market near the station. Neha held the spool of string.

For an hour the kite rose higher and higher. Then a strong wind blew in from the hills, the string snapped and the green kite floated away over the mango trees.

Arjun was upset. He had wanted to show the kite to his grandfather, who was coming from Nashik that evening. Neha said nothing, but after lunch she disappeared into her room with some coloured paper, two thin sticks and a pot of glue.

When Grandfather arrived at six o'clock, a new kite was waiting on the table. It was blue, not green, and its tail was made from the ribbon Neha used to wear in her school plait. Grandfather laughed and said it was the finest kite he had seen in years.

passages.title: A letter from Leh
passages.text:
Dear Isha,

Greetings from Leh! Papa's new job has brought us to Ladakh, and everything here is different from Pune. The town is high up in the mountains, so the air is thin. On our first day I felt tired after climbing only ten steps, and the doctor told us to rest for two whole days before doing anything else.

Our house has thick walls of mud bricks and a flat roof. In autumn, our neighbour, Mrs Dolma, spreads apricots on her roof to dry in the sun. She says the dried fruit will feed her family through the long winter, when snow closes the roads over the mountain passes and trucks cannot bring food up from the plains.

School starts at ten o'clock here, not eight, because the mornings are so cold. In winter we will have a holiday of nearly three months. Can you imagine a long holiday in the coldest season instead of the hottest?

I miss your mother's poha and our kabaddi games after school. Please write back and tell me whether the Diwali lamps are up in our building yet.

With love,
Mihir

passages.title: Raghu the driver
passages.text: Raghu drives his auto-rickshaw through the busy streets of Pune from early morning until late at night. He is the most cheerful driver on Laxmi Road. He hums old film songs while he waits at red lights, and he greets every passenger with a wide grin. When it rains, he keeps a dry towel on the seat so that children going to school do not get wet. "A smile costs nothing," he tells them as they climb in.

passages.title: Ajji's house in Konkan
passages.text:
Ajji's house stands at the end of a muddy path, under tall coconut trees. Its roof is made of red clay tiles that rattle when the monsoon rain beats down. Inside, the rooms are dark and cool, and they smell of wood smoke and ripe jackfruit. A swing made from a plank and two thick ropes hangs in the front verandah.

Ajji herself is small and quick. She is awake before the roosters, sweeping the courtyard with a broom of coconut leaves. She scolds the goats in a loud voice, but she slips them banana peels when she thinks nobody is watching.

passages.title: The new boy
passages.text:
On the first day after the Diwali holidays, a new boy called Farhan joined Grade 4. He stood by the door with his bag clutched against his chest and his eyes fixed on his shoes. When the educator asked him to tell the class about himself, he whispered his name so softly that only the front row heard it.

At break, Farhan sat alone on the steps and opened his tiffin very slowly, as if he hoped nobody would notice him. Sana and Dev were playing kabaddi nearby, and their team was one player short. Dev waved and called to Farhan to join them. Farhan shook his head, but Sana pulled him gently by the sleeve.

Ten minutes later he was the fastest raider on the ground, shouting "kabaddi, kabaddi" louder than anyone. When the bell rang, he was grinning, and his white shirt was covered in dust.

passages.title: The fort at night
passages.text:
When the bus finally stopped below Jaisalmer Fort, the sun had already sunk behind the dunes. Meher looked up at the walls. In the dusk they seemed enormous, dark and silent, like a giant crouching on the hill. A cold wind hissed through the narrow gate, and somewhere above, a door banged again and again. Meher held her brother's hand tightly and did not say a word as they climbed the steep, uneven steps.

At the top, everything changed. A man was lighting lamps along the lanes, and each little flame turned the yellow stone the colour of honey. Smells of roasting peanuts and warm bajra rotis drifted from an open kitchen. A grandmother sitting in a doorway waved at them and called out, "Come in, come in, you must be hungry after your journey!" Somebody was playing a tune on a stringed instrument, and two small boys were dancing to it in the street.

Meher let go of her brother's hand. For the first time since they had left Pune, she laughed.

passages.title: The rangoli
passages.text:
On Diwali morning, Tara and her little brother Om knelt outside their front door in Pune with five bowls of coloured powder. Slowly and carefully, they made a big rangoli of a peacock, with blue feathers and a bright orange beak.

Just as they finished, a gust of wind blew across the step and scattered half of the blue powder.

Om began to cry, but Tara fetched more powder. Together they turned the smudge into a row of little blue flowers, and Amma said it was even prettier than before.

passages.title: The cricket match
passages.text:
Every Sunday, the children of Shanti Nagar played cricket in the empty plot behind the temple.

This Sunday was special, because the team from the next lane had come to play them for a small silver cup. Rohan's side batted first and scored forty-two runs.

Then, in the very first over of the other team's turn, their only ball was hit over the wall into Mr Joshi's garden. Mr Joshi was known for keeping every ball that landed among his roses.

Rohan knocked on the gate and offered to water the roses every evening for a week. Mr Joshi smiled, handed back the ball and even stayed to watch the game.

Shanti Nagar lost by two runs, but that evening Mr Joshi invited both teams for lassi on his verandah.

passages.title: The night of the power cut
passages.text:
Mitali lived with her parents on the ninth floor of a tall building in Hadapsar. She loved the evenings, when she could see the lights of the whole city from the balcony.

One July evening, her parents went to a wedding and left her with her grandfather, who could not see well in the dark. They ate dal and rice together and played carrom while the rain drummed on the windows.

At half past eight, there was a loud crack of thunder and every light in the building went out. Grandfather's medicine was in the kitchen cupboard, and he needed to take it at nine o'clock.

Mitali remembered the torch in the drawer under the television. She felt her way along the wall, counting her steps as her father had taught her, found the torch and lit the way to the kitchen. Grandfather took his medicine on time.

When her parents came home at midnight, they found the two of them fast asleep on the sofa, with the torch still glowing between them.

passages.title: Why our town needs bees
passages.text:
Many people run away when a bee flies near them, but bees are among the most useful insects in the world. This report explains what they do for us and how we can help them.

Bees carry pollen from one flower to another as they collect nectar. Without this, plants such as mangoes, pumpkins and sunflowers could not make fruit or seeds.

Bees also make honey. A single bee makes only a tiny drop in its whole life, so one jar of honey is the work of thousands of bees.

Sadly, there are fewer bees than there used to be. Many gardens have lost their flowers, and some of the sprays used on crops harm them.

We can help by growing flowering plants such as tulsi, marigold and hibiscus on balconies and in school gardens. If every class in our school planted one pot, the bees of our town would have dozens of new places to feed.

passages.title: Camels of the Thar Desert (mixed up)
passages.text:
A. Finally, camels have clever ways of dealing with the sand. Their wide, padded feet stop them from sinking, and two rows of long eyelashes keep out the grains when the wind blows. They can even close their nostrils during a sandstorm.

B. So the next time you see a camel walking slowly across the dunes in Rajasthan, remember that every part of its body suits life in one of the harshest places in India.

C. In the Thar Desert, the days are burning hot, the nights can be freezing and water is hard to find. Yet one animal lives there with ease: the camel. This report explains how it copes with three problems: thirst, hunger and sand.

D. Next, hunger. Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water, but it is really a store of fat. When food is scarce, the camel's body uses this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and floppy.

E. First, thirst. A camel can walk for days without drinking. When it does find water, it can gulp down more than a hundred litres in about fifteen minutes.

passages.title: Stuck on the bridge
passages.text:
The bus had not moved for twenty minutes. In the middle of the narrow bridge ahead stood a large brown buffalo, chewing slowly and refusing to move. The driver honked, but the buffalo only flicked its ears.

It had been such a good morning until then. Class 4B of Green Valley School had left Pune at seven o'clock for a trip to Khadakwasla dam. As the bus climbed the hill road, the children sang so loudly that the driver joked he needed earplugs.

Now the songs had stopped. Some children were worried they would miss their picnic by the water, and Kabir was sure the buffalo would stay there all day.

Then Aarav, whose grandfather kept buffaloes in his village, had an idea. He collected the banana peels from everyone's tiffin boxes, walked onto the bridge beside Ms Pillai and held one out. The buffalo stretched its neck towards it, then followed him slowly to the far bank and settled happily in the long grass.

The class reached the dam an hour late, but they still had their picnic. On the way home, everyone cheered as the bus rolled across the empty bridge.

passages.title: Tulsi
passages.text: Many Indian homes keep a tulsi plant in a pot near the door or on the balcony, because tulsi is a very useful plant. Its leaves can be boiled in water with ginger to make a warm drink when someone has a cough. The leaves have a strong, sweet smell that keeps mosquitoes and other insects away. Some families also drop a few leaves into their drinking water to give it a fresh taste.

passages.title: Holi in our lane
passages.text:
Holi is the noisiest and most colourful day of the year in our lane in Pune. By eight in the morning, children are already running between the buildings with water pistols, and the grandparents are sitting on plastic chairs to watch. Somebody's uncle always plays loud music from a speaker on his balcony.

The festival also brings the neighbours together. Families who hardly speak during the year share gujiya and thandai, and old quarrels are forgotten with a smear of pink powder on the cheek. Mrs Kulkarni from the third floor even dances with the Sharma family, whose dog barks at her every other day of the year.

passages.title: Saving water in Pune
passages.text:
In April and May, before the monsoon arrives, many parts of Pune receive water from the taps for only a few hours a day. Tankers rumble through the streets, and families fill buckets, drums and bottles while they can. Water is precious in the hot months.

Small habits at home can save a surprising amount. Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth saves several litres each time. A bucket of water for a bath uses far less than a long shower, and the water used to wash vegetables can be poured on plants afterwards.

Some housing societies go further. They collect the rain that falls on their roofs during the monsoon and send it down pipes into the ground or into large tanks. This is called rainwater harvesting, and it means that the society has water stored for the dry months.

passages.title: The turtles of Velas
passages.text:
Every winter, a quiet beach at Velas, a fishing village on the Konkan coast, receives some special visitors. Female olive ridley turtles crawl out of the sea at night, dig a hole in the sand with their back flippers and lay about a hundred eggs. Then they cover the nest and return to the waves, never to see their young.

For many years, very few of these eggs hatched. Dogs dug them up, people collected them to eat, and crabs and birds took the rest. The turtles of Velas were slowly disappearing.

About twenty years ago, the villagers decided to change this. Volunteers began to walk the beach before dawn, move each new clutch of eggs into a fenced hatchery and guard it day and night. Today, when the babies hatch after about fifty days, the villagers carry them in baskets to the water's edge and watch them scurry into the sea.

Visitors now come from Pune and Mumbai to watch the hatchlings, and they pay to stay in village homes. In this way, the turtles have brought work to the village, and the village has given the turtles a future.

passages.title: A day at Shaniwar Wada
passages.text: Last Saturday our class visited Shaniwar Wada, the old fort palace in the middle of Pune. First we walked through the huge Delhi Gate, which has sharp iron spikes to stop elephants from pushing it open. Then our guide showed us the ruins of the rooms where the Peshwas once lived, and the lotus-shaped fountain in the garden. Before we left, we sat on the lawn and ate our tiffin under a big tree.

passages.title: The Ghats in the rain
passages.text:
When the monsoon reaches the Western Ghats in June, the hills change completely. Dry brown slopes turn bright green within a few weeks, and hundreds of waterfalls appear on the cliffs, some of them for only a few months of the year.

The rain also wakes up many animals. Frogs call loudly from every puddle, crabs climb out of the streams, and colourful snails slide slowly across the wet rocks.

People enjoy the season too. At weekends, families from Pune and Mumbai drive up to the hill stations to walk in the mist, eat hot roasted corn from roadside stalls and splash under the falls.

passages.title: Lunch on time
passages.text:
Every working day in Mumbai, thousands of office workers eat a hot lunch cooked in their own homes. The lunches reach them through the dabbawalas, a group of about five thousand delivery workers who have been carrying tiffins across the city for more than a hundred years.

In the late morning, a dabbawala collects tiffins from the homes in one area. Each tiffin is marked with letters, numbers and colours that show where it must go.

The tiffins travel on local trains, then on bicycles and handcarts. At each station they are sorted again, and new dabbawalas carry them on to the right office building.

The system is famous because it so rarely goes wrong. Visitors from other countries have come to study how the dabbawalas deliver so many lunches every day without computers or phones.

In the afternoon, the empty tiffins make the same journey home again.

passages.title: A walk to Nongriat
passages.text:
To reach the village of Nongriat in Meghalaya, you must walk down more than three thousand stone steps through thick, wet forest. It is one of the rainiest corners of India, and the path is often slippery with moss.

But the walk is worth it, because at the bottom you cross a bridge that nobody built with bricks or steel. It is made from the living roots of rubber fig trees, twisted together across a rushing stream.

The Khasi people who live here make these bridges slowly. They guide young roots across the stream along hollow trunks of bamboo or betel nut trees. Over fifteen to thirty years the roots grow thick and strong enough to carry people.

Unlike a wooden bridge, which rots in the heavy rain, a root bridge grows stronger as it gets older. Some are thought to be hundreds of years old. In Nongriat there is even a bridge with two levels, one above the other.

Today, the villagers are still planting and training new roots, so that their grandchildren will have bridges too.

passages.title: Making a rangoli for Diwali
passages.text: First, Amma swept the step outside our door and sprinkled it with water. Next, she drew a pattern of white dots with chalk. Then my sister and I joined the dots with lines of white powder to make the shape of a lamp. After that, we filled the spaces with red, yellow and green colours. Finally, Amma placed small clay diyas around the edge, and we lit them as soon as it grew dark.

passages.title: Rain at the bus stop
passages.text: Dhruv was waiting at the bus stop near Deccan when the first drops of the monsoon began to fall. He had not brought an umbrella because the morning had been bright. The rain grew heavier, so he stepped under the roof of a small tea stall. The stall owner was busy, but she found him a stool. She also gave him a cup of hot ginger tea, free of charge. By the time his bus came, the rain had eased to a drizzle. Dhruv thanked her twice and promised to bring her a box of his mother's laddoos the next day.

passages.title: Trees on our streets
passages.text:
Trees make city streets more pleasant. For example, one big rain tree can shade a whole bus stop, and the air beneath it can feel several degrees cooler than the open road nearby.

Trees are also homes. Mynas, parrots and squirrels nest in their branches, while ants and beetles live in the cracks of the bark.

However, many street trees are cut down when roads are made wider. As a result, some streets that were once green and shady are now hot and dusty. This means that planting new trees is more important than ever. In addition, people can protect old trees by building a low wall around their roots.

So, if we want cool and lively streets, we must look after the trees we have and plant new ones for the future.

passages.title: Salt from the sun
passages.text:
Much of the salt on India's tables comes from the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, a flat, empty land that is covered by sea water for part of the year. When the water goes down after the monsoon, families called Agariyas arrive to make salt.

First, they dig wells to reach salty water deep under the ground. Then they pump it into wide, shallow pans. Over the following weeks, the hot sun dries up the water, and white crystals begin to form.

This work is very hard. The workers rake the crystals every day in fierce heat, and the glare from the white salt hurts their eyes. Despite this, many families have made salt here for hundreds of years, and they take pride in it.

In recent years, some families have started to use pumps that run on sunlight instead of diesel. As a result, they spend less money on fuel and earn more for each load of salt they sell.

So the next time you sprinkle salt on your poha, remember the families who made it under the desert sun.

passages.title: The New Girl
passages.text: Kavya stood at the school gate, holding her tiffin box tightly with both hands. Her uniform was stiff and new, and her black shoes did not have a single scratch. Children ran past her, shouting to their friends, but nobody called her name. She looked down at the map of the school that her mother had drawn on a sheet of paper. Then a girl with two long plaits stopped and asked, "Are you in 4B too?" Kavya's shoulders dropped, and she smiled back.

passages.title: Up the Hill
passages.text: The bus wound up the hill for an hour before it stopped. When Arjun stepped down, his breath made little clouds in the air. Tall pine trees stood on both sides of the road, and somewhere below, a stream rushed over stones. A woman passed him with a bundle of sticks on her back, and two goats followed her without being told. There was no honking, no traffic signal and no shop with bright lights. Arjun pulled his jacket closer and zipped it up to his chin. His cousin Tashi was waiting at the bend, wearing a woollen cap pulled down over his ears. "You will need one of these," Tashi laughed, holding out a second cap that he had brought from home.

passages.title: The Empty Chair
passages.text: Every evening at six, Mr Joshi carried two plastic chairs out of his flat and set them under the gulmohar tree in the society garden. He sat on one and left the other empty. Children playing cricket nearby often hit the ball towards him, but he never complained. Instead, he picked it up, rubbed it on his trousers like a fast bowler and threw it back. One evening, Rohan noticed that Mr Joshi had brought two cups of tea, although nobody sat in the second chair. He kept glancing at the gate, then at his watch. When the street lights came on, he poured the second cup slowly into the flower bed, folded both chairs and went inside without a word. The next evening, Rohan left his bat by the wall, walked over and sat down in the empty chair. Mr Joshi looked surprised. Then he pushed a cup of tea towards Rohan and began to talk about a match he had played fifty years ago.

passages.title: Two Pots
passages.text: The well at the edge of Bhimsar was so deep that Leela could count to twenty before she heard the bucket splash. Every morning she and her mother walked there before the sun was high, each with two brass pots, and every morning they joined the line of women already waiting. Nobody in the line wasted a drop. When Leela's younger brother spilt half a pot while playing, her mother did not shout. She simply poured her own share into his pot and walked home with one pot instead of two. That evening the family scrubbed their plates with sand before rinsing them in a single bowl of water, and the bowl was then poured onto the tulsi plant by the door. Later, a visitor from the city stepped off the bus, asked for a glass of water and drank it in one gulp. He held out his glass for more. Leela's mother filled it again without a word, but Leela saw her glance at the nearly empty pot in the corner. Leela said nothing either. She only decided that tomorrow she would wake up earlier and make the walk to the well twice.

passages.title: The Sandcastle
passages.text: Neha and her little brother Kabir spent the whole morning building a sandcastle on the beach. They made four towers, a strong wall and a deep moat all around it. Neha kept looking at the sea. "The waves are coming closer every few minutes," she said. Kabir did not listen. He was busy pressing shells into the tallest tower. Just then, a big wave rushed up the sand, much further than the others, and filled the moat with foaming water.

passages.title: Grey Monday
passages.text: On Monday morning the sky over Pune was grey and heavy. Ishaan's mother held out his umbrella at the door, but Ishaan said it made his bag too heavy and left it on the shoe rack. At lunch break the clouds grew darker, and the wind began to pull at the leaves of the neem tree in the playground. By the last bell, thunder was rumbling and the first fat drops were falling on the dusty path. Ishaan's friend Zoya opened her bright yellow umbrella and looked at him. "My house is on your way," she said. "Walk with me." Ishaan looked at the long road home, then at the dark sky, and then at Zoya's umbrella.

passages.title: The Weak Spot
passages.text: A week before the kite festival, Grandpa showed Riya how to check her manja. "Run your fingers along the string," he said. "If you feel a rough patch, the string is weak there, and it will not last in a fight." Riya found one rough patch near the middle of her string, but she was too excited to wind on a new one. "It will be fine," she told herself. On the morning of Sankranti, she climbed onto the terrace with her red kite. Soon it was high above the rooftops, dancing beside dozens of others. Her neighbour Om's green kite came closer and closer until the two strings crossed. Om began to pull hard. Riya pulled back even harder. The strings rubbed against each other, faster and faster, right at the point where her string was rough.

passages.title: The Last Raid
passages.text: In the first half of the inter-school kabaddi final, Farhan was the best raider on the court. He touched three defenders in one raid and the crowd roared. But as he leapt back over the middle line, he landed awkwardly and limped to the bench, rubbing his ankle. The coach pressed an ice pack on it and shook her head. On the bench sat Dev, the smallest player in the team. All season he had been the first to arrive at practice and the last to leave, and every evening he practised his escape move against the wall of the school building until the watchman sent him home. Twice the coach had told him, "Your footwork is the quickest in this team. One day we will need it." With two minutes left, the other team was one point ahead. The coach looked at Farhan's swollen ankle, then down the bench. "Dev," she said. Dev stood up, tightened his shoelaces and walked to the middle line. The defenders smiled at one another when they saw how small he was, and they spread out lazily across the mat.

passages.title: The Guava and the Tiffin
passages.text:
Text A (a story): Two squirrels found one ripe guava under a tree. Each squirrel grabbed it and pulled. They pulled and pulled until the guava flew out of their paws and rolled into the pond. Neither squirrel ate anything that day.

Text B (a poem):
My tiffin has two parathas,
My friend's is bare today.
I give her one, she gives a grin,
And then we run to play.

passages.title: Two Brave Steps
passages.text:
Text A (a story): Meher stood at the edge of the swimming pool, her toes curled over the wet tiles. The deep end looked dark and endless. Her coach held out a float. "One length," he said. Meher took a breath, pushed off the wall and kicked until her hand touched the far side.

Text B (a diary): Friday. Today I had to say my poem on stage in the Hindi Day assembly. My knees were shaking and my mouth felt dry. I looked at Mum in the third row, and she nodded. I said every line without stopping. Everyone clapped. I am so glad I did not run away.

passages.title: The Extra Coin
passages.text:
Text A (a tale): Long ago, in a busy market town, there lived a fruit seller named Gopal. One evening a tired traveller bought six bananas and paid with a silver coin, not knowing it was worth far more than bananas. Gopal ran after him down the dusty road and gave the coin back. The traveller was a rich merchant. The next week he returned and bought all of Gopal's fruit for his daughter's wedding.

Text B (a school newsletter recount):
Lost Purse Returned at Diwali Fair
On Saturday 1 November, Class 4C ran the lucky-dip stall at our school Diwali fair. At four o'clock, Aditi Rao found a purse under the table. Inside were some notes and a bus pass. Aditi took it straight to the help desk instead of keeping it. The owner, a grandmother from Kothrud, thanked her with a box of sweets, which Class 4C shared at the end of the day.

passages.title: The Neem Speaks
passages.text:
Text A (a poem):
I am the neem by the school gate,
I have stood here eighty years.
I shade the children while they wait,
I hear their laughs and tears.
They say a road will come this way,
They say my roots must go.
Who will cool the gate in May?
Who will tell the crows hello?

Text B (an information leaflet):
Plant a Tree This Monsoon
One grown neem tree can cool the air around it by several degrees. Its leaves trap dust, and birds and squirrels nest in its branches. This July, the Pune Green Club will give away 500 saplings at the city garden. Each family can take two saplings, a bag of compost and a card that shows how to plant and water them. Volunteers will show children how to dig a small pit and press the soil firmly around the roots. Last year, more than 300 families took part. Come between 8 a.m. and 12 noon on Sunday 13 July. Please bring a cloth bag to carry your saplings home.

passages.title: When Aaji Was Young
passages.text: When Aaji was a girl in a small village near Satara, there was no electricity in her house. Every evening her father lit a kerosene lantern and hung it on a nail by the door. Aaji did her homework on a slate, and when she finished, she wiped it clean with a damp cloth. Once a month, a postman came on a bicycle with a letter from her uncle in Bombay. The whole family sat together on the floor to hear it read aloud.

passages.title: The Boat to School
passages.text: Anu lives in a village in Kerala where the land is criss-crossed by long green canals called backwaters. Her house stands on the bank, and coconut palms lean over the water outside her window. Every morning at seven, she climbs into a small wooden boat with five other children. Old Thomas pushes the boat along with a long bamboo pole, and the children wave to the women washing clothes on the stone steps. When the monsoon rains are heavy, the canal rises so high that the boat glides right past the tops of the bushes. Anu's school has no bus and no car park. It has a small jetty instead, where the boats tie up in a neat row.

passages.title: The Only Radio in the Lane
passages.text: It was the summer of 1965, and the whole lane in Shaniwar Peth seemed to be squeezed into the Kulkarnis' front room. Their radio was the only one on the street. It was a big wooden box with two round knobs, and it had to warm up for a whole minute before any sound came out. Shobha sat on the floor between her brothers, waiting for the cricket score. Outside, a tonga clattered past, the horse's bells jingling. Her mother had queued at the ration shop all morning for rice and sugar, and now she was making tea on the brass stove in the corner. When the announcer finally spoke, the room went silent. Nobody had a television, and the newspaper would not bring the score until the next morning. So everybody leaned towards the crackling voice, and when India took a wicket, twenty people cheered at once.

passages.title: Monsoon of 1946
passages.text: In the monsoon of 1946, the village of Kelshi on the Konkan coast had no electricity yet, and the nearest town was a whole day away by bullock cart. Every morning before dawn, Sumati helped her mother grind rice into flour on the heavy stone wheel in the courtyard. Then she carried the brass pot to the well, balancing it on her head the way her grandmother had taught her. School was a single room above the temple, where twenty children of every age sat on mats and copied letters onto slates. In the evenings, the family sat around a small oil lamp while her father mended fishing nets. Her brother switched on the television to watch the news from the city. When a letter arrived from her uncle in Bombay, it was a week old, and the whole street came to hear it read. Sumati dreamed of seeing Bombay one day, with its trams and tall buildings, but for now her world was the beach, the well and the paddy fields turning green in the rain.

passages.title: Diwali Morning
passages.text: I woke up before the sun on Diwali morning. My little sister was still asleep, so I tiptoed past her to the balcony. The whole building was quiet. I lit the first diya and placed it on the step. Then Aai came out with the box of rangoli colours, and we drew a big lotus by the door. By the time my sister woke up, our lotus was finished and the diyas were glowing.

passages.title: The Lost Ball
passages.text: Rahul kicked the football too hard, and it flew over the wall of the garden. He climbed onto a brick and peeped over. The ball was sitting in Mrs Desai's flower bed, right next to her prize roses. Rahul's face went red. He walked round to her gate and rang the bell. Mrs Desai came out, looked at the ball and then at Rahul, and laughed. She handed it back with a rose for his mother.

passages.title: Kabaddi After School
passages.text: She ran to the playground as soon as the bell rang. Every afternoon, Pallavi and her friends played kabaddi on the dusty patch behind the school hall. Today the teams were even, and the score was tied for a long time. Pallavi took a deep breath, chanted loudly and raced across the line. She touched two players on the shoulder and slipped out of their arms before they could hold her. Her team jumped up and down, cheering. Pallavi was covered in dust from head to toe, but she did not care at all. Her grin was the widest on the playground.

passages.title: Our Trip to the Fort
passages.text: We left school at seven in the morning, two buses full of excited children. Our class was going to Sinhagad Fort for the day. The road curled round and round the hill, and Manav felt sick, so we gave him the window seat. At the top, the wind was so strong that it nearly blew off my cap. Our guide showed us the old stone gates and the place where soldiers kept watch long ago. For lunch we ate hot pithla bhakri at a small stall, and then we raced each other back to the buses, tired and happy.

passages.title: The Holi Plan
passages.text: Two days before Holi, the children of Sai Park met under the water tank to make a plan. "I will bring the colours," said Aryan, waving a bag of green and pink powder. "I will fill the water balloons," said Fatima. "We should not throw anything at Ajoba this year," whispered Tanya. "He told my mother the colours hurt his eyes last time." Everyone went quiet. They all liked Ajoba, the old man on the ground floor who fixed their bicycles for free. On Holi morning, the children played until they were purple and green from head to toe. When Ajoba stepped out of his door, nobody threw a single balloon. Instead, Tanya walked up and gently put a dot of yellow on his forehead with one finger. Ajoba smiled, took a pinch of red from her bag and dabbed it on her cheek. "Happy Holi," he said.

passages.title: The Missing Notebook
passages.text: "Pooja, have you seen your science notebook?" Mum called from the kitchen. I had not. I looked under my bed, behind the cupboard and in every pocket of my school bag, but it was nowhere. My stomach turned over. The notebook had my whole project on the water cycle, with the diagram I had coloured so carefully. My brother Neel stood in the doorway, holding his cricket bat. "Is it blue, with a cloud sticker on the front?" he asked. I nodded. He pointed at the dining table, where it was propping up one short leg of the table. Mum had used it on Sunday when the table wobbled. I pulled it out, and the table rocked. We all burst out laughing, and Mum promised to buy a proper rubber wedge.

passages.title: Old Yellow
passages.text: For twenty-two years I have carried people through the streets of Pune. My paint was bright yellow and black once, but now it is faded, and there is a long scratch down my side from the day a cow wandered into the road. Ganesh has driven me every one of those years. He starts each morning by wiping my mirrors with an old cloth and hanging a fresh string of marigolds above his seat. He hums old film songs when the traffic is slow, and he never charges extra when it rains, even though other drivers do. Today he stopped beside a girl in a school uniform who was crying at the bus stop. She had missed her bus, and her exam started at nine. Ganesh did not ask for money. He simply nodded at the seat behind him. I rattled and coughed up the flyover as fast as my old engine allowed. We reached her school gate at two minutes to nine. She waved as she ran in, and Ganesh patted my handle as if to say, well done, old friend.

passages.title: Aaji's Story
passages.text: The power had gone out, and the rain was drumming on the tin roof. Tanvi and her cousins sat close together around the candle, and Aaji pulled her shawl tight. "When I was your age," Aaji began, "I walked three kilometres to school every day, and I crossed a river on a log. One morning in the monsoon, the river was so full that the log had gone. I stood on the bank and cried, because I had never missed a single day. Then my friend Kamal arrived with her father, and he carried both of us across on his shoulders, one on each side." The cousins laughed at the picture of two little girls riding across a river. Tanvi looked at her grandmother's thin hands and tried to imagine them holding on to a farmer's shoulders in the rain. "Did you get to school on time?" she asked. Aaji smiled. "Wet to the knees," she said, "but on time." Just then the lights flickered back on, and everybody groaned because the story was over.

passages.title: Lost at the Mela
passages.text: The mela was full of noise and colour. Siya held her mother's hand as they walked past the bangle stalls and the giant wheel. Then Siya stopped to watch a man making balloon animals. When she turned round, her mother was gone. Siya's heart thumped. All she could see were strangers' legs. She remembered what her mother had told her and walked straight to the police booth by the gate. Ten minutes later, her mother came running and hugged her tight.

passages.title: Summer at the Farm
passages.text: Every May, when school closed, Yash went to stay at his grandparents' farm near Nashik. There was no lift, no traffic and no television in the evenings. Instead, there were mango trees to climb and a buffalo called Kali who liked to have her neck scratched. Yash woke at six to the sound of the cockerel and helped his grandfather carry fodder to the shed. In the afternoons it was too hot to work, so everyone lay on mats under the trees and ate mangoes until the juice ran down their elbows. On his last night, Yash sat on the roof with his grandmother and counted more stars than he had ever seen in Pune. He did not want to go home.

passages.title: Picked Last
passages.text: Every lunch break, the two captains chose their cricket teams in the same way, and every lunch break Sahil was picked last. He was not fast, and he usually missed the ball when he batted. He always smiled and said he did not mind, but he walked to his team very slowly. One Thursday, the ball was hit high towards the boundary. Everyone shouted, "Catch it!" Sahil ran, tripped over his own feet and fell flat on his back. The ball dropped straight into his hands as he lay on the grass. For a moment nobody moved. Then his whole team rushed over, pulled him up and lifted him onto their shoulders. The next day, the captain who usually picked first pointed at him straight away. "Sahil," he said. Sahil tried not to grin too widely, but he could not stop himself.

passages.title: The Island Girl
passages.text: Mariam had lived all her life on a small island in Lakshadweep, where she could walk from one shore to the other in half an hour. She knew every fisherman by name, and she swam in the clear blue lagoon every evening. When her father got a new job, the family moved to Pune. On her first day at her new school, Mariam felt as if she had landed on another planet. There were more children in her class than in her whole island school, and the traffic outside roared all day. At lunch, a boy asked her where her island was, and when she told him, he said, "I have never even seen the sea." Mariam stared at him. She could not imagine a life without the sea. That weekend, she drew a map of her island, with the lagoon, the lighthouse and her grandmother's house, and pinned it above her new bed. On Monday she brought a shell to school and put it in the boy's hand. "Hold it to your ear," she said. He did, and his eyes went wide.

passages.title: Green Valley School Mela
passages.text:
Come to the Green Valley School Mela!
The mela is on Saturday 6 December from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. There will be twelve food stalls and a rangoli competition. Tickets cost twenty rupees. I think the games stall is the most exciting part of the mela. Our dhokla is the tastiest in Pune! All the money will help to buy new library books. You will love it!

passages.title: Ganesh Lassi House
passages.text:
Ganesh Lassi House
Cool down this summer at Ganesh Lassi House, near the main gate of Laxmi Road market. We are open every day from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Our sweet lassi costs thirty rupees a glass, and our mango lassi costs forty. We make our curd fresh every morning in our own kitchen. In our opinion, nothing is better on a hot afternoon than a tall glass of mango lassi. Our kesar kulfi is simply delicious, and children will find our rose milkshake wonderful. We also sell packets of poha and samosas. Bring your friends, because lassi tastes best when you share it!

passages.title: Review: The Clever Crow
passages.text:
Review: The Clever Crow, a play by Class 5
by Ritika, Class 4A
On Friday, Class 5 performed The Clever Crow in the school hall. The play lasted forty minutes, and twenty-six children were in it. It tells the story of a crow who outwits a greedy fox to save her nest. Ahmed played the fox, and Divya played the crow. In my view, Ahmed was the funniest actor on the stage. The costumes were made by the parents, and the fox wore a long orange tail made of wool. I think the songs were too long, but the dance in the forest scene was brilliant. The play ended with a loud drum roll. It is the best play our school has put on this year, and I would give it four stars out of five. Everyone should see it when it is performed again next month.

passages.title: Review: Shinde's Snack Corner
passages.text:
Food Review: Shinde's Snack Corner, Deccan
by Ira, Class 4B, for the school magazine
Shinde's Snack Corner has been selling misal pav on the same corner since 1978. The shop has six tables, and on Sundays people queue outside for half an hour. Mr Shinde's daughter now runs the kitchen, and in 2019 her misal won first prize at the city food fair. A plate costs sixty rupees and comes with two soft pavs and a bowl of curd. Honestly, the misal is far too spicy for children. My father, however, says it is perfect. The pavs were warm, and the curd cooled my mouth down quickly. A small fridge of cold drinks stands next to the counter, and the waiters are the friendliest on the whole street. The walls are painted bright orange and covered with old photographs of Pune. It is a cheerful place, although it can get very noisy. Every family in Pune should try it at least once. If you cannot handle spice, ask for the mild misal, which is made only on request. The shop is closed on Tuesdays.

passages.title: The Diwali Rangoli
passages.text: On the morning of Diwali, Tara woke up early. Her grandmother was already in the courtyard with a basket of bright powder. They swept the floor and drew a large circle with white chalk. Tara filled the petals with orange and pink colour. Her little brother Om wanted to help, so she gave him a small spoon of yellow powder. He sprinkled it carefully around the edge. A gentle breeze blew, and some powder flew onto the steps. Om laughed and clapped his hands. When the rangoli was finished, Grandmother lit tiny clay lamps and placed them around it. The neighbours stopped to admire the pattern. Tara felt proud because they had made it together.

passages.title: How Rice Grows
passages.text: In many villages near Pune, farmers wait for the monsoon before they start work in the fields. When the first heavy rain arrives, the dry ground turns soft and brown. If the rain is late, the farmers have to be patient. Farmers plant seeds and water them by hand. Young rice plants are bright green and very tiny. After a few weeks, the farmers move them into flooded fields. They work in rows, pressing each plant into the mud. The light from the lamps helps the farmers work at night. Frogs croak loudly in the wet fields, and egrets hunt for insects between the plants. By the end of the season, the green plants turn golden. The farmers cut the rice, tie it in bundles and carry it home. It is hard work, but every family is glad when the harvest is safe.

passages.title: The Peacock
passages.text: The peacock is the national bird of India. A male peacock has a long tail of green and blue feathers. The female bird is called a peahen. She is brown and has a short tail. Peacocks eat seeds and insects. They often dance when the monsoon rain begins.

passages.title: Three Festivals
passages.text: Diwali is the festival of lights. It comes in October or November. Families light small clay lamps called diyas and draw rangoli patterns at the door. Holi comes in spring, in March. Children throw coloured powder called gulal and splash water at each other. Eid comes at the end of Ramzan, a month of fasting. Families wear new clothes and share a sweet dish called sheer khurma with their neighbours.

passages.title: The Indian Elephant
passages.text: The Indian elephant lives in forests and grasslands in many parts of India, such as Kerala and Assam. It is smaller than the African elephant and has smaller ears. An elephant uses its trunk to smell, to drink and to pick up food. It eats grass, leaves, bark and fruit, and it can eat for sixteen hours in a day. Elephants live in family groups called herds. The oldest female leads the herd. A baby elephant is called a calf. It stays close to its mother for many years. Elephants can live for about sixty years.

passages.title: The Camel and the Yak
passages.text: The camel and the yak both help people carry heavy loads, but they live in very different places. The camel lives in hot, sandy deserts, such as the Thar Desert in Rajasthan. Its hump stores fat, which gives it energy when food is hard to find. Long eyelashes keep the sand out of its eyes, and wide, flat feet stop it sinking into the sand. A camel can go for many days without water. The yak lives high in the cold mountains of Ladakh. It has long, thick hair that keeps it warm in the snow. Its strong lungs help it breathe where the air is thin. People drink yak milk and make warm cloth from its hair. Both animals are gentle, but a camel may spit when it is cross.

passages.title: The Thirsty Crow
passages.text: One hot afternoon, a crow flew over the dry fields near the village. He was very thirsty, but every pond had dried up. At last he saw a clay pot under a tree. There was a little water at the bottom, but his beak could not reach it. The crow thought hard. He picked up a pebble and dropped it into the pot. Then he dropped another, and another. Slowly the water rose to the top. The crow drank happily and flew away.

passages.title: Meera's Kite
passages.text: On the morning of Makar Sankranti, Meera ran up to the terrace with her new red kite. Her brother Kabir held the reel of string while she let the kite rise into the bright sky. Soon it was dancing above the rooftops with hundreds of other kites. Suddenly a gust of wind pulled it sideways, and the string tangled in the branches of the neem tree next door. Meera tugged, but the kite would not move. Kabir wanted to climb the tree, but Meera stopped him because the branches were thin. Then their neighbour, Mr Joshi, came out with a long bamboo pole. Carefully, he lifted the string free. Meera thanked him and flew her kite again until sunset.

passages.title: The Lost Tiffin
passages.text: Arjun was the quietest boy in Class 4, but he always noticed things that others missed. On the class trip to Sinhagad Fort, he carried his tiffin box carefully in his bag. Inside were his mother's soft theplas and a small box of mango pickle. When the class stopped to rest near the old stone walls, Arjun put his bag down and went to look at a tiny lizard on a rock. When he came back, his bag was open and the tiffin box was gone. Arjun did not want to make a fuss, so he said nothing. Then he noticed a trail of crumbs leading behind a wall. He followed it quietly and found a young monkey with his tiffin box, licking pickle from its fingers. Arjun laughed so loudly that the whole class came running. That lunchtime, his friends Zoya and Dev shared their food with him, and everyone agreed that the monkey had the best lunch of all.

passages.title: The Potter's Wish
passages.text: Long ago, in a village beside the river Mula, there lived a potter named Gopal. Every day he sat at his wheel and shaped clay into pots, lamps and cups. His pots were so strong that people came from far away to buy them, but Gopal was never happy. "If only I were rich like the merchant," he sighed, "then my life would be perfect." One evening, an old woman stopped at his stall. She was tired and dusty from her journey, so Gopal gave her a cup of water from his best pot. The woman smiled. "You have a kind heart," she said. "For this, I will grant you one wish. Think carefully before you speak." Gopal's eyes shone. He thought of gold, of a big house, of fine clothes. Then he looked at his wheel and the rows of pots drying in the sun. He thought of the children who came to watch him work, and the families who cooked in his pots. At last he spoke. "I wish that my hands may always make things that help people." The old woman nodded and walked away into the dusk. From that day, Gopal hummed as he worked, and he never wished to be the merchant again.

passages.title: The Indian Peafowl
passages.text: The peafowl is the national bird of India. The male is called a peacock and the female is called a peahen. Peacocks have long tails of shining blue and green feathers. When it rains, a peacock spreads its tail like a fan and dances. Peafowl live in forests and farms. They eat seeds, insects, small snakes and berries. At night they sleep high up in trees, where they are safe from wild cats.

passages.title: Lassi
passages.text: Lassi is a cool drink made from curd. It first came from the Punjab region, where farmers drank it after long hours in the hot fields. Today people all over India enjoy it, especially in summer. Sweet lassi is made by whisking curd with sugar and a little water. Salted lassi has salt and roasted cumin instead of sugar. Some cooks add mango pulp to make mango lassi, which is a favourite with children. Lassi is often served in a clay cup called a kulhad, which keeps it cold. Curd is good for the stomach, so lassi is healthy as well as tasty.

passages.title: The Monsoon in India
passages.text: The monsoon is a season of heavy rain that comes to India every year. It usually reaches the coast of Kerala in early June and spreads north across the country over the next few weeks. Pune often gets its first monsoon showers in the second week of June. The rain is carried by strong winds that blow from the Indian Ocean. These winds pick up water as they cross the warm sea and drop it as rain when they meet the land and hills. The monsoon is very important for farmers, because crops such as rice, cotton and sugarcane need plenty of water. It also fills the lakes and dams that give cities their drinking water. However, too much rain can cause floods, and roads can turn into rivers. By the end of September, the winds change direction and the monsoon slowly leaves the country.

passages.title: Sinhagad Fort
passages.text: Sinhagad is a hill fort about thirty kilometres south-west of Pune. It stands on a steep hill more than thirteen hundred metres high, and on a clear day visitors can see the Khadakwasla lake shining far below. The fort was once called Kondhana. Its walls were built along the edge of the cliffs, so enemies found it very hard to climb up. The most famous story about the fort is from 1670, when the brave warrior Tanaji Malusare and his soldiers climbed the cliffs at night to capture it. Tanaji lost his life in the battle, and the fort was given a new name, Sinhagad, which means Lion's Fort. Today Sinhagad is a popular place for families and school groups. Visitors can walk up a winding path or travel most of the way by road. At the top they can see the old gates, water tanks cut into the rock and a memorial to Tanaji. Many people stop at small stalls to eat hot pithla bhakri and drink buttermilk before they walk back down. It is best to visit in the cool months, from October to February, because the path can be slippery in the monsoon.

passages.title: Making a Rangoli
passages.text: On the morning of Diwali, Priya and her mother made a rangoli at their front door. First, they swept the floor and sprinkled it with water. Next, Priya drew the outline of a lotus with white chalk. After that, they filled the petals with pink and yellow powder. Then her mother added a border of tiny green dots. Finally, they placed small clay lamps around the edge. When the lamps were lit that evening, the whole doorway glowed.

passages.title: Growing a Bean
passages.text: Rohan wanted to grow a bean plant for the science fair. To begin with, he soaked a bean in water overnight. The next morning, he wrapped it in a wet tissue and put it in a glass jar. Two days later, a tiny white root pushed out of the bean. Soon after, a green shoot appeared at the top. When the shoot was as long as his finger, Rohan planted the bean in a pot of soil. By the day of the fair, it had four leaves.

passages.title: Our Trip to the Zoo
passages.text: Last Friday, Class 4 went on a trip to the zoo at Katraj. As soon as we arrived, we saw the white tiger resting in the shade. After that, our guide took us to the snake park, where a keeper showed us a python. At midday we ate our tiffin under a big banyan tree. Later, we watched the elephants splashing in their pool. Before we left, everyone bought a postcard at the gate. We were tired but happy on the bus home.

passages.title: The Rainy Day Match
passages.text: Every Sunday, Kavya and her friends played cricket in the lane behind their building. One Sunday in July, dark clouds rolled in just as the match began. Soon heavy rain was pouring down, and the lane filled with puddles. The children were disappointed. Then Kavya had an idea. She invited everyone to her flat, and they played a game of carrom instead. By the evening, they all agreed that it had been the best Sunday of the monsoon.

passages.title: The New Girl
passages.text: Nandini was the new girl in Class 4B. She was tall, with two long plaits tied with red ribbons. She was shy at first, but she was very kind. On her first day, she shared her tiffin with Omkar, who had forgotten his. Nandini loved drawing birds, and her notebook was full of parrots and kingfishers. When the educator asked about her old school, she smiled and said, "I miss my friends, but I think I will like it here."

passages.title: Uncle Faiz's Shop
passages.text: Uncle Faiz ran the smallest shop on Laxmi Road, but it was the busiest. He was a round man with a grey beard and glasses that slid down his nose. He knew every child's name and always slipped an extra toffee into their bags. "A sweet day starts with a sweet," he liked to say. His niece Rukhsar helped him after school. She was quick at sums and could add up a whole bill in her head before Uncle Faiz found his calculator. She dreamed of becoming a pilot and kept a paper aeroplane on the shelf above the till. When the shop was quiet, she read books about famous flights, while her uncle hummed old songs and dusted the jars of sweets.

passages.title: The Kabaddi Match
passages.text: Coach Sharma blew his whistle and the Class 4 kabaddi team ran onto the muddy field. Leading them was Aditya, the captain, who was the fastest runner in the school. He was small and wiry, with a scar on his chin from an old fall, and he never stopped smiling. "We play fair, and we play together," he told his team before every match. Behind him came Pooja, the tallest girl in the class. She was strong but nervous, and she chewed the end of her plait when she was worried. Last came Sameer, who joked all the time. He made everyone laugh, even Coach Sharma, but he always helped the younger children tie their laces before a game. When the match began, Pooja froze. Aditya ran to her side and whispered, "You are our best defender. Just hold on." Pooja nodded, took a deep breath and stopped the raider with both arms. The team won by three points, and Sameer danced all the way back to the classroom.

passages.title: The Lantern
passages.text: Every night, old Ramu walked around the city museum with his lantern, though the lights had been electric for years. He wore a khaki coat two sizes too big and boots that squeaked on the marble floors. The young guard, Vikram, laughed at the lantern. "Kaka, the whole building is lit up. Why carry that old thing?" Ramu only smiled. "Lights go out. A flame does not forget." Vikram spent most nights playing games on his phone. One stormy night in July, thunder cracked over the city and every light in the museum went dark. Vikram's phone battery was nearly finished. In the black hallway, he heard footsteps and a soft scraping near the room of old coins. His hands shook. Then a warm yellow glow came round the corner. Ramu held up his lantern, and its light fell on a thief with a bag full of silver coins. The thief dropped the bag and ran straight into the arms of the police, who had come when Ramu rang the brass alarm bell by the door. The next morning, Mrs Kulkarni, who ran the museum, thanked both guards. Vikram looked at the floor. "It was all Ramu Kaka," he said quietly. "From tonight, I am carrying a lantern too."

passages.title: Kiran and the Cave of Bats
passages.text: Kiran had always wanted to see the old cave behind her grandfather's village. One morning, she packed a torch, a rope and two bananas, and set off up the hill. The path was steep and slippery after the rain. At the mouth of the cave, hundreds of bats flapped past her head. Kiran took a deep breath and stepped inside. The cave was dark and cold. Suddenly, she heard water rushing in behind her. The stream was rising fast! Kiran tied her rope to a rock and climbed onto a high ledge. From there she saw a thin line of light. She crawled towards it and squeezed out through a gap into the sunshine. 'What a day!' she laughed, as she ran home to tell her grandfather.

passages.title: The Peacock and the Crow
passages.text: A peacock lived beside a village pond. Every day he spread his shining blue and green feathers and laughed at the crow. 'Look at you,' he said. 'You are plain and black. Nobody stops to look at you.' The crow said nothing and went on with her work, picking up scraps and keeping the fields clean. One evening, a great storm came. The peacock's long feathers grew heavy with rain, and he could not fly up to the safe branches of the tree. The crow flew down, cawing loudly, and woke the farmer, who carried the peacock into his shed. The next morning, the peacock bowed his head to the crow. Being kind is worth more than being beautiful.

passages.title: Two Stories
passages.text:
Story 1: How the Peacock Got Its Eyes
Long ago, the peacock had plain brown feathers. One day, the god of the sky lost his hundred shining jewels in a forest. The peacock searched all night and found every one. The god was so pleased that he set the jewels in the peacock's tail as a gift. That is why a peacock's feathers have bright eyes on them to this day.
Story 2: The Case of the Missing Tiffin
On Monday, Neel's tiffin box vanished from his desk. Detective Pooja looked carefully around the classroom. She found a trail of crumbs leading to the window, and a small paw print on the sill. 'Who left the window open?' she asked. Meera put up her hand. Pooja peeped outside and smiled. Under the tree, a fat monkey was eating Neel's parathas!

passages.title: Two Stories
passages.text:
Story 1: The Goat Who Would Not Share
On a dry hill outside Satara, a goat rested in the shade of the only tree. A tired calf asked if she could share the shade. 'No,' said the goat. 'This shade is mine.' As the day went on, the sun moved across the sky, and the shade moved too. Soon the goat was sitting in the hot sun, and the calf was cool on the other side of the tree. Lesson: share what you have, for tomorrow you may need help.
Story 2: Storm on the Sea
Asha and her uncle were fishing on the Arabian Sea when the sky turned black. Thunder crashed! Waves as tall as houses smashed into their little boat, and the mast snapped in two. 'Hold on!' shouted Uncle Joseph. Asha grabbed the lantern and swung it high again and again. At last, a beam of light swept across the water from the lighthouse at Ratnagiri. A rescue boat roared towards them through the rain.

passages.title: Two Stories
passages.text:
Story 1: The Robot Who Could Not Laugh
In the year 2150, Riya lived with her family on a base on Mars. Her best friend was Bolt, a silver robot who cleaned the dusty windows. Bolt could do sums faster than any computer, but he could not laugh. Every evening, Riya told him jokes, and every evening Bolt simply blinked his blue lights. One night, a dust storm broke the base's power. Bolt led the families to safety through the dark tunnels, using his own lights. When Riya hugged him, a strange new sound came from his speaker. Bolt was laughing! Friends come in all shapes, even metal ones.
Story 2: The Message at the Fort
Three hundred years ago, a boy named Tanaji lived in a village below a stone fort in the Sahyadri hills. One night, he saw torches moving through the forest. Enemy soldiers were coming! Tanaji ran up the steep steps of the fort, past the cannons and the tall wooden gate, to warn the guards. They closed the gate just in time. In the morning, the captain gave Tanaji a silver coin, and the whole village cheered.

passages.title: Honeybees
passages.text:
Did you know that a honeybee has five eyes? These busy insects are found all over India.
What they look like
A honeybee has a striped yellow and brown body, two pairs of wings and six legs.
Food
Bees drink nectar from flowers. They also collect pollen to feed their young.
Homes
Honeybees live together in a hive. One hive can hold thousands of bees, but only one queen.
Why they matter
When bees move from flower to flower, they carry pollen. This helps plants make fruit, such as mangoes and apples.
Fun fact: To make one spoonful of honey, bees must visit thousands of flowers!

passages.title: Our Trip to Sinhagad Fort
passages.text: Last Saturday, our class went on a trip to Sinhagad Fort near Pune. We met at school at seven o'clock and climbed onto the bus. First, we drove up the winding road to the bottom of the fort. Then we walked up the stone steps to the top. It was hard work, and I was out of breath! At the top, our guide told us how soldiers once guarded the fort. After that, we sat on the wall and ate our tiffin while clouds floated past below us. Finally, we walked down and rode the bus back to school. It was the best day ever!

passages.title: Two Texts About Mangoes
passages.text:
Text 1: Mango Lassi
You will need: one ripe mango, a cup of curd, half a cup of cold milk and two spoons of sugar.
1. Peel the mango and cut it into pieces.
2. Put the mango, curd, milk and sugar into a blender.
3. Blend until smooth.
4. Pour into glasses and serve cold.
Text 2: Why Do Mangoes Turn Yellow?
A green mango is hard and sour. First, the mango grows on the tree until it is fully grown. Then it starts to give off a gas that begins the ripening. Because of this gas, the green colour slowly fades and the yellow underneath shows through. At the same time, the starch inside turns into sugar, so the fruit becomes soft and sweet. That is why a ripe mango is yellow and juicy.

passages.title: How to Make a Paper Boat
passages.text:
On a rainy day, a paper boat is fun to sail in a puddle. Follow these steps to make your own.
You will need
• a large sheet of paper
• crayons to decorate it
What to do
1. Fold the paper in half from top to bottom.
2. Fold the top corners down to the middle to make a triangle.
3. Fold the bottom strips up on both sides.
4. Open the shape from the middle and press it flat into a square.
5. Fold the bottom corners up, then gently pull the top points apart.
6. Shape your boat and decorate it.
Now take it outside and watch it float!

passages.title: Hide and Seek
passages.text:
Characters: DEV, a boy of eight; NANI, his grandmother; PINKY, his sister
(A sitting room. A long curtain hangs by the window.)
PINKY: Quick, Dev! Nani is coming!
DEV: (whispering) Where can I hide?
PINKY: Behind the curtain. Hurry!
(Dev hides behind the curtain. His feet stick out at the bottom.)
NANI: (walking in slowly) Where is that boy? I have hot jalebis for him.
DEV: (jumping out) Here I am, Nani!
NANI: (laughing) I could see your toes all along, my dear.
PINKY: Dev, you are the worst hider in the whole of Pune!
(They all laugh and sit down to eat.)

passages.title: The Green Leaf News
passages.text:
The Green Leaf News
Class 3B, Sunrise Primary School, Pune
Sports Day
Our Sports Day will be held on 14 December on the big ground. There will be running races, a sack race and a tug of war. Parents are welcome to come and cheer. Things to remember for Sports Day: wear white clothes, bring a water bottle, come by eight o'clock and bring a cap.
Our Library
This month, Mrs Joshi has put twenty new books on the library shelves. There are joke books, books about space and a new set of adventure stories. You can take home two books each week.
Lunch Time
Last Friday, every class planted a tree near the school gate. Class 3B planted a neem tree and gave it a name: Neemu. We will water it every morning.

passages.title: The Late Train
passages.text:
CHARACTERS
AJJI, a grandmother
ROHIT, her grandson, aged nine
STATION MASTER
SCENE 1: A railway platform in Pune, early in the morning.
(AJJI sits on a bench with a big cloth bag. ROHIT walks up and down.)
ROHIT: (looking at the clock) Ajji, the train should be here by now!
AJJI: Patience, Rohit. Trains are like monsoon clouds. They come when they are ready.
ROHIT: (sighing) But we will be late for Mama's wedding!
(The STATION MASTER enters, waving a green flag.)
STATION MASTER: The Kite Express is running ten minutes late. Please stay behind the yellow line.
ROHIT: Ten minutes! That is forever!
AJJI: (opening her bag) Then let us eat a laddoo while we wait.
(ROHIT sits down and smiles. A whistle sounds far away.)
ROHIT: (jumping up) Listen, Ajji! It is coming!
AJJI: (laughing) You see? Ready, at last.

passages.title: Making a Clay Diya
passages.text: Before Diwali, our class made clay diyas to take home. It was messy but great fun, and you can make one too. To make a diya you need a ball of clay about the size of a lemon, a little water in a bowl, a pencil, some paint and a brush. First roll the clay into a smooth ball between your hands. Then press your thumb into the middle to make a hollow. Pinch one side to make a little spout for the wick. If the clay cracks, wet your fingers and smooth it. Use the pencil to draw a pattern around the edge. Leave the diya in the sun for two days until it is dry and hard. Finally paint it in bright colours and let the paint dry. Ask an adult to help you put in the wick and light it.

passages.title: Monsoon in Maharashtra
passages.text:
Monsoon in Maharashtra
Every year, from June to September, the monsoon brings heavy rain to Maharashtra. Farmers wait for it eagerly, because their rice, sugar cane and cotton crops need the water. Towns and cities need it too, to fill their lakes and wells.
Where the rain comes from
In summer, the land heats up faster than the sea. Warm, wet winds blow in from the Arabian Sea. When they reach the Sahyadri hills, they rise and cool, and the water falls as rain. The hills and the coast get the most rain.
Fact box: Some places in the hills get more than five metres of rain in one season!
Getting ready for the rain
Things to pack in your school bag:
1. a raincoat
2. a small towel
3. a plastic cover for books
4. a spare pair of socks
When it floods, stay indoors. Keep away from fallen wires. Boil water before you drink it. Listen to the radio for news.
Caption under a photo: Children wade home through a flooded street in Kolhapur.

passages.title: Monsoon in Pune
passages.text:
Paragraph 1
The monsoon reaches Pune in June. Dark clouds fill the sky, and heavy rain falls for hours. The streets turn into little rivers, and frogs croak all night. Thunder booms and lightning flashes over the hills. The air feels cool and damp, and everything turns green. Sometimes the rain stops for a few days, and then it pours again.
Paragraph 2
We wear raincoats and gumboots to school. After school, my brother and I sail paper boats in the puddles. The river near our house rises and turns brown. In the evening, Aai makes hot bhajis and tea, and we eat them by the window. On weekends, we visit the waterfalls near Lonavala with our cousins. We always come home soaked and happy.

passages.title: The Banyan Tree
passages.text:
Paragraph 1
The banyan is the national tree of India. It is huge, with a thick trunk and wide, spreading branches. Its leaves are large, shiny and leathery, and its small red figs grow in bunches.
Paragraph 2
A banyan tree grows in a surprising way. Its seed often begins life high up on another tree, where a bird has dropped it. Roots grow down from its branches like long ropes. Many villages hold their meetings in the shade of a banyan. When the roots touch the soil, they thicken into new trunks. In this way, one banyan can slowly spread over a whole field.
Paragraph 3
People in India value the banyan. Its deep shade keeps travellers cool on hot afternoons. Some banyan trees are hundreds of years old, and people visit them like old friends. Birds, bats and squirrels find food and shelter in its branches.

passages.title: A Letter to Sofia
passages.text:
Dear Sofia,
Thank you for your letter and the photos of the snow in your town. I have so much news to tell you, so I am writing a long letter this time.
In June, I started at a new school in Pune. It is much bigger than my old one, and it has a library with thousands of books. My class has thirty-two children, and I sit next to a girl called Ira, who is now my best friend. Last week, we celebrated Holi. In the morning, Ira and I threw coloured powder at each other until we looked like rainbows. In the afternoon, my grandmother made puran poli, a sweet flatbread, for the whole street.
Next month, my family is going to visit my uncle in Goa. We will travel by train along the coast, and I hope to see the sea for the first time.
Please write soon and tell me what you did in your holidays. Do you have a festival with colours too?
Your friend,
Anika

passages.title: A Day at Splash Valley
passages.text:
Looking for the perfect way to beat the summer heat? Then Splash Valley, just outside Pune, is the place for you! My family spent a whole Sunday there in May, and none of us wanted to leave.
The park has twelve slides. The tallest one, called the Thunder Tube, is a thrilling drop that made my little brother scream with joy. The wave pool is warm and gentle, so even small children can splash safely. The staff were kind, the rides were thrilling and the food was fresh and tasty, but the queues were long.
Tickets cost 400 rupees for children, which is not cheap, but I think the day is worth every rupee. The park opens at ten o'clock, so go early to avoid the crowds.
My rating: 4 stars out of 5. You will have the best day of your summer, I promise!

passages.title: Jungle Trail Camp: an Advert and a Review
passages.text:
The Advert
Do your children love adventure? Send them to Jungle Trail Camp in the hills near Mahabaleshwar! Our camp is never crowded and our snacks are cheap. Every child gets their own tent, and our expert guides keep everyone safe. Your child will come home happier, braver and full of stories, we promise! 9 out of 10 children say it is the best week of their lives! Book now: only 20 places left!
The Review, by Farah, aged 10
I went to Jungle Trail Camp in October. The guides were friendly, and the night walk to see the fireflies was magical. However, the camp was very crowded, and I had to share my tent with three other girls. A packet of chips cost 80 rupees, which my dad said was far too much. The food at dinner was good, though. I would give the camp 3 stars out of 5. It was fun, and I made two new friends, but it was not the best week of my life.
